title: Your short videos are losing people before the point arrives
markdown:
# Your short videos are losing people before the point arrives

At 9:17 p.m., you trim a 28-second video down to 19 seconds, add captions, pick a cover, and post it. The next morning, the view count has moved, but the retention graph has already fallen off a cliff. People did not reject your idea. Most of them never stayed long enough to hear it.

That first beat is a separate writing job. A good video can still open with the part a viewer has learned to skip: "Hey guys," a slow setup, an apology for being late, or a promise that the useful bit is coming. On a feed, "coming" is often too late.

This article gives you a way to find the weak spot, write better opening lines, and test them without pretending one clever sentence will rescue every video.

## Find the sentence that gives viewers permission to leave

Play your video with the sound off and stop at the three-second mark. What has the viewer received? If the answer is only your name, the topic, or a vague announcement, the opening has made them wait for the payoff.

Compare these starts:

- "Today I want to talk about why your reels are not growing."
- "If your reel starts with 'today I want to talk about,' you have already spent the three seconds people were willing to lend you."

The second line is not magic. It names a familiar mistake, puts the consequence beside it, and makes a small promise: this video knows why the viewer is frustrated. It also gives the rest of the clip a job. You now need to show the fix, not repeat the accusation.

Your strongest raw material is usually already in the video. Look for one of these:

- a costly mistake the viewer is making;
- a specific before-and-after change;
- an unpopular choice you can defend;
- a result that needs an explanation;
- a detail that creates a question your video can answer.

Avoid borrowing a dramatic hook that has nothing to do with the footage. "I almost quit" may get a pause, but it burns trust if the video is a tutorial about lighting. The opening should set the right expectation for the next 15 seconds.

## Write hooks as options, not as one precious line

Creators often get stuck because they try to write the definitive hook before recording. That is like choosing a thumbnail before you know what the video proves. Write several versions after the core idea is clear.

Start with one plain sentence: "This video shows freelance editors how to make a client revision request less vague." Then turn the same idea in different directions:

- "The revision request that wastes the most time is usually one sentence long."
- "If a client says 'make it pop,' send this question before you open the timeline."
- "I stopped taking vague revision notes at face value. Here is the question that changed the work."

These alternatives do different work. The first creates recognition. The second promises a usable move. The third has a personal angle, which only works if the video genuinely tells that story. Pick the one your footage can immediately support.

If you need help generating options without falling back on the same recycled formulas, [Hook Lab is a ready-made prompt for writing short-form hooks](https://promptbase.com/prompt/hook-lab-win-the-first-3-seconds-2?via=keipanda&ct=capafy-distribute-promptbase-hook-lab). Give it the audience, the video idea, and the friction your viewer feels. Treat its output as a stack of drafts. Keep the lines that sound like something you would say out loud, then rewrite the rest.

## Make the picture and the first line agree

An opening line has to survive the screen, too. If you say, "This is why your product demo loses people," do not begin with a logo animation. Begin with the moment that proves it: a cursor clicking through five empty screens, a hand hovering over a skip button, or the awkward first sentence typed into a script.

Captions can carry the hook when viewers are muted, but they should not merely duplicate a rambling spoken introduction. Put the tension in the first visible words. Keep them short enough to read while the image changes.

There is also a timing problem. A useful opening often needs a half-beat of context, but it cannot spend that half-beat clearing its throat. Record the hook twice: once as the first sentence, and once after you cut the first few words. The trimmed version is frequently the one that sounds like a person getting to the point.

## Test the opening without fooling yourself

Do not call a hook a winner because it feels sharp in your notes app. Publish comparable videos or re-cut the same idea when that fits your workflow. Watch early retention alongside the comments and the kind of viewer the post brings in.

One result is noisy. A hook can draw the wrong people, a strong topic can carry a weak opening, and a familiar audience may tolerate a slow start that strangers will not. Keep a small record of the line you used, the video topic, the opening visual, and what happened in the first few seconds. After a handful of posts, you will see which promises you can deliver well.

The goal is not to trick a thumb into pausing. It is to make the first three seconds honest enough that the right person wants the next three. When the hook and the video agree, you have a better chance of earning the rest of the watch.
